title: Imagine being known for the worst thing you’ve ever done.
paragraphs: Imagine being known for the worst thing you’ve ever done.
That was Paul.
Before he became the missionary who carried the Gospel across the Roman world, he was the man Christians feared the most.

He didn’t just oppose the church.
He hunted it.
Scripture tells us that Paul approved of the death of Stephen. He dragged believers from their homes. He imprisoned followers of Jesus. His name was associated with persecution, fear, and suffering.
So when Paul arrived in Jerusalem claiming he had become a follower of Christ, the disciples didn’t celebrate.
They stepped back.

Acts 9 tells us they were afraid of him.
They didn’t believe he was truly a disciple.
Can you imagine the tension in that moment?
A room full of believers who had every reason not to trust him.
A man with a past so dark that even his testimony sounded unbelievable.
Paul had encountered Jesus on the road to Damascus. His life had completely changed. But transformation does not erase reputation overnight.
And sometimes the hardest thing to rebuild is trust.
But then one man stepped forward.
Barnabas.

Barnabas listened to Paul’s story.
Barnabas believed his testimony.
Barnabas took Paul and personally brought him to the apostles.
In other words, Barnabas put his own reputation on the line for a man everyone else was afraid of.
That moment may seem small in the story of the early church, but it changed history.

Because Paul would go on to preach the Gospel across nations.
He would plant churches throughout the Roman Empire.
He would write letters that still shape the faith of millions today.

Romans.
Galatians.
Ephesians.
Philippians.
Colossians.
But before the missionary…
Before the apostle…
Before the writer of half the New Testament…
Paul was simply a man nobody trusted.
And Barnabas was the man who believed him.
Sometimes we assume the people who change the world are the ones on the stage.
But Scripture quietly reminds us that some of the most powerful people in God’s story are the ones who stand beside someone else and say,
“I believe God is working in you.”

Barnabas didn’t write the letters Paul wrote.
He didn’t travel the same missionary routes Paul traveled.
But he played a role that was just as important.
He opened a door.
One encourager can unlock a destiny.
Think about how many people today are stuck behind the walls of their past.

People who have truly changed…
but no one believes them.

People who have repented…
but everyone still remembers who they used to be.

People who have a calling…
but they’re waiting for someone to give them a chance.
Barnabas teaches us something powerful about the Kingdom of God.
Encouragement is not a small ministry.
It is destiny-shaping work.
Sometimes the greatest thing you can do for someone is not preach to them, correct them, or control them.
Sometimes the greatest thing you can do is believe that God really has changed them.
And maybe that’s the question this story leaves us with.
Who is the “Paul” in your life?
Who is the person that others are hesitant to trust… but God may be transforming?
And what if your belief in them could unlock the next chapter of their calling?
Because sometimes the difference between a forgotten calling and a fulfilled destiny…
is one person willing to stand up and say:
“I believe God has changed you.”

Acts 9:26–27
“When he came to Jerusalem, he tried to join the disciples, but they were all afraid of him… But Barnabas took him and brought him to the apostles.”
Someone out there may need a Barnabas in their life today.
